record.summary: A voluntary Code of Practice setting baseline cyber security requirements for AI systems, including generative AI, against AI-specific risks such as data poisoning, model obfuscation and indirect prompt injection. Its 13 principles span five lifecycle phases, from secure design to secure end of life, and assign provisions to developers, system operators and data custodians, among them capabilities for human oversight, security testing before release and deployment, monitoring of system behaviour, and incident management and recovery plans. It is meant as the basis of a global ETSI standard.
record.notes: Published with an implementation guide that DSIT commissioned and that DSIT and NCSC officials reviewed. The Code is an addendum to the Software Code of Practice and builds on the NCSC's Guidelines for Secure AI Development of November 2023; 80% of respondents to DSIT's call for views, held from 15 May to 9 August 2024, endorsed the intervention. DSIT, with the NCSC, will submit the Code and the guide to ETSI as the basis for a new global standard (TS 104 223) and implementation guide (TR 104 128), and the government will update the Code to mirror the ETSI standard.

verification.note: Stored and read in this run: the Code's GOV.UK HTML text (published 31 January 2025; scope, audience, the 13 principles and their provisions) and the GOV.UK publication page (stored as the secondary source; DCMS and DSIT, published 31 January 2025 with no later update, the implementation guide and the ETSI plan). Snapshots of 11 Oct 2026, unchanged on 17 Oct. Whether ETSI has since published TS 104 223, and whether the Code was updated to mirror it, is not in a stored file; the publication page showed no update on 11 Oct 2026.

legal_force.quote: The scope of this voluntary Code of Practice is focused on AI systems.

summary.quote: This includes systems that incorporate deep neural networks, such as generative AI.
These include security risks from data poisoning, model obfuscation, indirect prompt injection and operational differences associated with data management.
we have separated the principles into five phases. These are secure design, secure development, secure deployment, secure maintenance and secure end of life.

summary.locator: Structure of the voluntary Code of Practice
summary.quote: Principle 13: Ensure proper data and model disposal
4.1 When designing an AI system, Developers and/or System Operators should incorporate and maintain capabilities to enable human oversight.
9.1 Developers shall ensure that all models, applications and systems that are released to System Operators and/or End-users have been tested as part of a security assessment process.
9.2 System Operators shall conduct testing prior to the system being deployed with support from Developers.

summary.locator: Structure of the voluntary Code of Practice

summary.quote: 6.5 Developers and System Operators shall create, test and maintain an AI system incident management plan and an AI system recovery plan.
This involves the development of a voluntary Code of Practice which will be used to help create a global standard in the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI)

safety_topics.locator: Structure of the voluntary Code of Practice
safety_topics.quote: Principle 9: Conduct appropriate testing and evaluation

safety_topics.locator: Structure of the voluntary Code of Practice
safety_topics.quote: Principle 4: Enable human responsibility for AI systems
4.3 Where human oversight is a risk control, Developers and/or System Operators shall design, develop, verify and maintain technical measures to reduce the risk through such oversight.

8.1 Developers shall document and maintain a clear audit trail of their system design and post-deployment maintenance plans. Developers should make the documentation available to the downstream System Operators and Data Custodians.
10.1 System Operators shall convey to End-users in an accessible way where and how their data will be used, accessed and stored

notes.quote: DSIT commissioned John Sotiropoulos, Senior Security Architect at Kainos and co-lead of the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, to create this implementation guide. Each iteration was reviewed by DSIT and NCSC officials.
AI stakeholders should view this document as an addendum to the Software Code of Practice.
This document also builds on NCSC’s Guidelines for Secure AI Development which were published in November 2023
The proposed intervention was endorsed by 80% of respondents to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology’s (DSIT) Call for Views which was held from 15 May to 9 August 2024.

DSIT, in close collaboration with NCSC, will submit the Code and the implementation guide in the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) where it will be used as the basis for a new global standard (TS 104 223) and accompanying implementation guide (TR 104 128).
The Government will update the content of the Code and Guide to mirror the future ETSI global standard and guide.
